title: RIZPAH WAS SAUL’S CONCUBINE—THEN ANOTHER MAN WAS ACCUSED OF SLEEPING WITH HER
paragraphs: RIZPAH WAS SAUL’S CONCUBINE—THEN ANOTHER MAN WAS ACCUSED OF SLEEPING WITH HER

She was introduced in Scripture in the middle of a sexual accusation between powerful men. Years later, she would be found beneath the bodies of her dead sons, fighting off birds and beasts. But if you read her story only for the scandal, you will miss the woman—and perhaps miss something painfully familiar about yourself.
Her name was Rizpah.
And the first time many people really notice her in the Bible, she is standing in the shadow of an accusation she did not make.
Not a love story.
Not a wedding.
Not a beautiful introduction.
An accusation.

The kingdom was fractured. Saul was dead. David was becoming stronger while the house of Saul was becoming weaker. Abner, commander of Saul’s army, had become enormously influential within the fading dynasty.
Then one sentence detonated inside Saul’s house.
The Hebrew text of 2 Samuel 3:7 says:
“וּלְשָׁאוּל פִּלֶגֶשׁ וּשְׁמָהּ רִצְפָּה בַת־אַיָּה”
Ule-Sha’ul pilegesh, u-shemah Ritzpah bat-Ayyah.
In straightforward English:
“Now Saul had a concubine, and her name was Rizpah, daughter of Aiah.”
Then comes the accusation:
“מַדּוּעַ בָּאתָה אֶל־פִּילֶגֶשׁ אָבִי”
Maddua ba’ta el-pilegesh avi?
Literally, the language asks why Abner had “gone in to” his father’s concubine—a conventional biblical expression referring to sexual relations.
Ish-bosheth, Saul’s son and the king supported by Abner, was confronting the most powerful man holding his kingdom together.
Why have you gone in to my father’s concubine?
And suddenly Rizpah’s body was at the center of a political explosion.
But there is something we must refuse to do if we want to handle Scripture faithfully.
We must not say more than God has said.
The Bible tells us that Ish-bosheth accused Abner.
It tells us Abner became furious.
It tells us the accusation contributed to a catastrophic break between Abner and Saul’s house.
But the narrative never pauses to give us a verdict saying, “Yes, Abner did it.”
Nor does it explicitly say, “No, the accusation was false.”
That silence matters.
Because sometimes careless Bible teaching turns an accusation into a conviction.
Scripture does not give us permission to do that.
And there is another silence that is even harder to ignore.
Rizpah does not speak.
Read the confrontation.
Ish-bosheth speaks.
Abner speaks.
Kingship is discussed.
Loyalty is discussed.
Betrayal is discussed.
Power is discussed.
But the woman whose body is at the center of the controversy?
No recorded words.
We are not told what Rizpah thought.
We are not told what Rizpah wanted.
We are not told whether she was consulted.
We are not told whether she wept.
We are not told whether she was terrified.
We are not even told, in this passage, what happened from her perspective.
And that should make us careful.
Because Rizpah is a real woman in the biblical narrative, not raw material for our imagination.
We should not invent conversations God did not record.
We should not manufacture motives the text does not reveal.
We should not transform biblical silence into fictional certainty.
But we can notice the silence.

And perhaps that is where her story begins reaching through the centuries and touching people who know exactly what it feels like to have everyone discussing what happened around them while almost nobody asks what happened inside them.
Maybe that is why this story hurts.
Because some people know what it is to become a sentence in somebody else’s argument.
Some know what it is to have their reputation discussed in rooms they never entered.
Some know what it is to become attached to a scandal they did not create.
Some know what it is to be remembered by what somebody else allegedly did.
Your name became connected to the divorce.
The betrayal.
The pregnancy.
The addiction.
The arrest.
The family breakdown.
The church controversy.
The affair.
The abuse.
The rumor.
The failure.
And suddenly people stopped seeing a human being.
They saw a story.
Rizpah’s story warns us how easily human beings can do that.
But there is more happening here than sexual scandal.

In the world of ancient monarchy, access to a deceased king’s concubines could carry political significance. Royal women could become entangled with questions of succession and claims to royal authority. That helps explain why Ish-bosheth’s accusation was not merely a private complaint about sexual morality. It could be heard as a challenge touching the throne itself.
That context makes Abner’s rage easier to understand.
He had been strengthening Saul’s house.
Now Ish-bosheth had accused him of wrongdoing involving Saul’s concubine.
Abner responded furiously and swore that he would help transfer the kingdom from Saul’s house to David.
One accusation.
One furious confrontation.
And political history moved.
Yet Rizpah remained Rizpah.
Not merely “Saul’s concubine.”
Not merely “the woman Abner was accused of sleeping with.”
A woman with a name.
A daughter.
“Rizpah, daughter of Aiah.”
And years later Scripture brings her back.
When it does, you may never forget her again.
There was famine during David’s reign.
The narrative connects the crisis with bloodguilt associated with Saul’s actions against the Gibeonites. After David consulted the Gibeonites, seven male descendants of Saul were handed over to them.
Among those seven were two sons of Rizpah.
Armoni.
Mephibosheth—the son of Saul and Rizpah, not Jonathan’s son of the same name whom David had earlier shown covenant kindness.
Imagine reading their names if you were their mother.
These were not statistics to her.
These were sons.
The men were killed and their bodies exposed.
Then the Bible gives us one of its most haunting pictures of maternal grief.
Rizpah took sackcloth.
She spread it upon a rock.
And she stayed.
From the beginning of the harvest until rain fell.
Day after day.
Night after night.
The birds came.
She drove them away.
The animals came.
She would not let them have the bodies.
The woman whose voice Scripture never records now performs an act so powerful that her actions reach the king.
Do not romanticize this scene.
It is horrifying.
A mother is beneath the exposed remains of her children.
There is no sentimental soundtrack.
No painless inspirational ending.
There is grief.
Heat.
Night.
Wild animals.
Birds.
Sackcloth.
Rock.
And a mother who refuses to abandon the dead.
How many nights did she stare into darkness?
Scripture does not tell us.
How many tears?
We do not know.
What prayers did she pray?
The Bible does not record them.
So we will not invent them.
But Scripture tells us what she did.
She stayed.
And eventually word reached David.
That detail is breathtaking.
Rizpah had almost no political power that the narrative tells us about.
She commanded no army.
Issued no decree.
Sat on no throne.
Yet her persistence became news powerful enough to reach the king.
David then acted.
He retrieved the bones of Saul and Jonathan and gathered the remains of those who had been exposed. They were buried in the tomb of Kish, Saul’s father.
The disgraced dead received burial.
And Rizpah’s vigil was remembered.
Do you see the strange arc of her biblical story?
She first appears while powerful men argue over her.
She reappears when powerful decisions have taken her sons.
In the first scene, men speak and Rizpah is silent.
In the later scene, Rizpah still has no recorded speech...
but everybody eventually hears what she is doing.
There are moments when faithfulness becomes a kind of testimony even before a sentence is spoken.
And maybe somebody reading this needs that.
Maybe you have spent years believing that because nobody heard your side, God did not see your side.
Those are not the same thing.
Human beings can overlook you.
God cannot lose sight of you.
Human beings can reduce you to your worst chapter.
God knows the whole book.
Human beings may remember the accusation.
God knows the truth.
And here we must go farther than Rizpah.
Because Rizpah can move us deeply, but Rizpah cannot save us.
Only Jesus Christ can.
The Bible is not ultimately a collection of inspirational survivors teaching us to become strong enough to rescue ourselves.
Scripture leads us to the Savior.
And when we reach Jesus, we meet Someone who knows what it means to be publicly accused, humiliated, condemned, exposed and treated as shameful.
But there is a crucial difference.
Jesus was sinless.
He did not merely become another tragic victim of human cruelty.
He willingly gave Himself according to the saving purpose of God.
At the cross, the innocent Son of God bore sin for sinners.
“For our sake he made him to be sin who knew no sin...” says 2 Corinthians 5:21.
First Peter 2:24 says Christ “bore our sins in his body on the tree.”
That is where this story must ultimately take us.
Not merely to a grieving mother sitting beneath death.
To the cross where death itself met its Conqueror.
Rizpah guarded bodies she could not resurrect.
Jesus walked out of His tomb.
That changes everything.
Christian hope is not that we can somehow protect everything we love from death.
We cannot.
Christian hope is that Jesus Christ has entered death, defeated it through His resurrection, and promises eternal life to those who belong to Him.
Maybe your scandal is different from Rizpah’s.
Maybe nobody knows yours.
You have learned how to smile around it.
You go to work.
You answer messages.
You attend church.
You post pictures.
You tell people, “I’m okay.”
But there is a rock somewhere inside your soul where you have been sitting for years.
Guarding what was lost.
Fighting memories.
Fighting shame.
Fighting bitterness.
Fighting the voice that says your story ended when everything fell apart.
Listen carefully.
Jesus did not come merely to make respectable people slightly better.
He came to save sinners.
He came for the guilty who repent.
For the ashamed who come into the light.
For the broken who know they cannot repair themselves.
For the exhausted.
For the hidden.
For people with chapters they wish could be ripped from the book.
The Gospel does not say your sin does not matter.
It says your sin mattered enough for Christ to die.
Grace is not God pretending evil is harmless.
Grace is God providing in Christ what guilty people could never provide for themselves.
Forgiveness.
Reconciliation.
A new heart.
A new allegiance.
A new life.
That is why repentance is beautiful.
Repentance is not cleaning yourself up so Jesus will tolerate you.
It is turning from sin and coming to the Savior because you finally understand that hiding cannot heal you.
Maybe you have spent years protecting your reputation while your soul was starving.
Maybe you know Christian vocabulary but have never surrendered to Christ.
Maybe you can quote verses and still secretly love the sin that crucified your conscience.
Maybe you have confused being around Christianity with belonging to Jesus.
Come to Christ.
Confess what you have hidden.
Turn from what is destroying you.
Believe the Gospel.
There is mercy in Jesus that your worst night cannot exhaust.
There is cleansing in Christ deeper than the stain you thought would define you forever.
There is no scandal so powerful that the grace of Jesus becomes powerless.
That does not mean every earthly consequence disappears.
It does not mean every relationship is automatically restored.
It does not mean repentance erases the temporal damage caused by sin.
It means something greater.
Your final identity does not have to be written by your rebellion, your shame, your suffering, somebody else’s accusation, or somebody else’s sin against you.
Jesus Christ can write redemption where you thought only ruins remained.
That is why our heartbeat is simple:
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
And if this exposed something you have been hiding from God, stop pretending He cannot see it.
He already sees.
Come into the light.
Somebody reading silently may need to discover that grace still reaches people in real life.
Not because clicking “Share” somehow earns favor with God. It does not. We are saved by grace through faith, not by social-media activity.
Someone may know Rizpah’s silence.
Someone may know scandal.
Someone may know grief.
Someone may desperately need to hear that Jesus still receives repentant sinners.

Supporting Gospel work does not purchase God's favor, prove your salvation, or make you more righteous before Him. Christ alone is our righteousness. But generous, willing support can help biblical teaching reach people who desperately need it.
But never confuse supporting a ministry with supporting the Gospel itself.
The Gospel does not need your money to become true.
Jesus is already Lord.

The question is whether His grace has taken hold of you so deeply that your time, your voice, your resources, your influence, your repentance, your generosity, and your entire life increasingly belong to Him.
It is surrender.
If you share, let it be mission rather than performance.
If you comment, let it be honest.
And whatever you do, do not leave Jesus outside the story.
Because Rizpah’s story eventually leaves us with a woman sitting beside death, unable to reverse it.
The Gospel takes us somewhere Rizpah could never take herself.
To an empty tomb.
To a risen King.
To Jesus Christ.
And perhaps the sentence you need to carry with you tonight is this:
The chapter that made people whisper your name does not have the authority to write the final sentence over a life surrendered to Jesus.
